sentences.text: This meeting is being recorded.
Howard.
Hey, Andy.
I, I can hear you, but I can't see you.
There you go.
Oh, there you are.
Sorry about that.
No worries, no worries.
How's it going?
Yeah, not too bad, thank you.
Not too bad.
I just sent out a newsletter just before.
Not this call, the one before, and I've just had like a deluge of responses, so.
Which doesn't always happen, but this one is particularly.
Must have been a good.
What was the topic of the, of the newsletter to warn all those responses?
Yeah, so we basically launched the opportunity to list your company on agencies co as a merge target.

So obviously there's a lot of agency owners that would like to do some kind of transaction, but they don't want to, you know, they don't want to borrow $1.2 million and acquire another business necessarily.
But they do do something.
They want to grow and they've hit a ceiling.
So we've, we've, we've launched merge basically as an option.
So now we've got a lot of companies that want to merge all of a sudden.
So.
Interesting.
What is, what is that entail?
Do they commit to who they want to merge with or just that they're interested in merging in general?
Yeah.
So it's.
Well, so the basic approach is to list as an opportunity for somebody else to merge with.
So there are a lot of.
I mean, obviously we talk to agency owners every single day.
There's a lot of agency owners that just don't want to sell.
They don't want to sell.
But also they've hit a ceiling or they're a bit burnt out, they're feeling alone.
And this is opportunity for them to find almost like a co founder, you know, a partner to go into business with and double the size of the business.
But not only that, they were.
They're also leveraging multiple arbitrage as well.
So they're able to sell eventually together for a much higher multiple than they would alone.
So it's a, you know, it's a good opportunity and nobody really does it.
Not certainly not the bottom end of the market.
Yeah, but that's where most agencies are.
They kind of, Most agencies don't ever get over the sort of 5 million hump.
So.
Yeah, and so what is your, what is your role in terms of facilitating that in a merger?
How would, how do you monetize that transaction?
So, yeah, there's different tiers.
The free tier or the cheap tier would be them for facilitating themselves.
But I mean, there's only a certain amount of guidance.
I think a lot of, a lot of M and A professionals are kind of gatekeepers.
Like there, there's this magic kingdom of M and A and it's totally mystical and unlike anything else that anybody in business does.
And it's, it just isn't true.
I, I find it just fascinating how strange people find M and A, but actually it's just really straightforward.
You're just, I mean if you're acquiring another company or just literally paying money for a business instead of starting it and it's as complicated as that.
Yeah, I, I, I hear you.

I, at the same time, having been on the sell side three times myself, there's a lot to it, there's definitely a lot of, and you know, if you're a firm, most of the people that you're probably talking to are founders, not necessarily private equity or professional buyers and sellers of businesses.
Just the process can be very time consuming, you know, very emotional, very distracting from the business running the day to day business.
Yeah, usually, Yeah.
I mean obviously we work on the buy and the sell side, so we work on the sell side as well.
We are working with private equity directly as well and also we sell to, you know, some fairly big companies as well.
Yeah, I mean it's a, it's a, it's a process for sure.
And certainly you need another set of eyes on it.
And it does depend on size and complexity.
Obviously it gets more and more complex the larger it gets.
I don't know what size companies you solve, but I should imagine anything that's over kind of sort of 5 or 10 million.
Around that mark it starts to get a little bit more hairy.
Yeah, but certainly I wouldn't buy anything that big without advisors.
When you say 5 to 10 million, you're talking top line or bottom line.
Around the top line it starts to get more complex.
Yeah.
Around the 5 to 10 mark, that's where most agencies top out and most agencies never make it past that, you know.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, I mean, what's what, you know, I've been following your LinkedIn posts and I don't think I'm subscribed to your newsletter, although I should and would welcome your input on mine.
I started one in January called Event Business Intelligence and it's each week it's a deep dive into a different topic.
Growth M and A.
Innovation, measurement, that kind of thing.
I've been speaking to a lot of.
So just to back up a little bit, my focus and background is on the events or, or experiential or meeting planning.
Side of the agency world and I've probably spoken to I don't know, maybe 50 to 75 different agency owners over the last few months.

You know every day I speak to a few others different, different things just to kind of they call me to reach out and bounce ideas off of me and you know, I also check in to see how they're seeing business develop and you know, what their growth plans are, et cetera.
And I've got a lot of interest from people looking to potentially sell their business or buy a business.
And I joined a mid market investment bank in January called Oakland's which has about 800 different bankers in maybe 40 countries.
And I joined the one in New York, Oaklands Da Silva and Phillips but I'm in a senior advisor role there.
Oh it's not, it's not full time, there's nothing paid up front.
Everything is sort of, you know, eat what you kill.
And they were looking to grow their event sector practice.
You know they, I think in February they sold a destination management company CSI to HIG Capital as part of a.
They combined two agent, two DMCs.
They had also acquired 360 in December.
It's helpful to get a sense of how they operate.
Their threshold though is pretty high.
They're looking for transactions with a fee of around a million dollars.

While I've come across a few of those and I've got a couple in the pipeline, the vast majority of the people I'm speaking to and the owners are would sell for transactions that would be hard pressed to justify a million dollar fee.
And so I'm sort of struggling in figuring out what's the best opportunity for that.

And I'm working on a couple on my own, you know and I've, I've told Oakland look, you know, if these, these things are too small for you, I'm going to work on them on my own and provide guidance and counsel.
In some cases it's consulting, some cases it's search or negot.

I mean it's, I'm still a little bit early in the process but you know when I saw your, your, your video or your note on LinkedIn about a potential roll up million dollar EBITDA, you know I'm, I come across a fair amount that are in that range and I'm trying to figure out what to do with them and how to help facilitate this.

So just as an example, like I'm talking to a guy owns a creative event agency in New York, does about a million million two in EBITDA Looking to sell, you know, he's, he'll find buyers but you know, at a certain multiple.
Last week I was at the Experiential Marketing Summit in Las Vegas and ran into somebody I know who has a literally an identical size business also looking to sell.
Those two would be well suited to potentially merge and then exit at a much higher multiple, you know, a mini version of the roll up that you discussed.
And so, you know, but at the same time I, I haven't done those before and you know, you gotta line up the funding for that and you know, figure out how to, how to get paid at the same time.
And so, you know, I thought it'd be good to reach out and just have another touch base and see.
Well, let me explain how, how you can, how, because I think it's quite straightforward.
So, so basically in this scenario there's a couple of ways you can do it, but one is with capital.
So that you would do it, you'd raise the capital of somebody, you'd acquire both and then integrate the two businesses over a period of time.
You would hope that there would be some organic growth as well as putting the businesses together and helping them refer internal clients to each other.
And the other way is what's called a virtual roll up, which you could easily do in this scenario.
So for you as the advisor, you would set up a holding company which has trigger agreements with both of these companies.
So you don't acquire them, you just get them to agree to sell to you at a certain price.
And then the trigger is when you sell a holding company that you then are able to purchase the two businesses.
So let's say most of these businesses around 1 to 2 million EBITDA, they're going to get a 5x multiple.
So you have a trigger agreement with both the companies to buy them at 5x or 5 million if that's what they're worth.
And then you go to market with the holding company so you can speak to other larger events agencies.
I think given your background it'd probably be easier for you to, to do that.
Or you could just go direct to private equity and you're selling the combined business for 8, 9, 10 times multiple.
Particularly if it's private equity and you can get over like 3 or 4 million EBITDA with the two businesses, then you can definitely start to scale the economics as well.
So the play would be for you to get paid on the uplift.
So if these two businesses are worth 10 million separately, if you sell them for 5 million, for instance, you would take 20% of the uplift.
But under that scenario you're, you're suggesting funding the initial acquisitions.
No, there's no acquisition.
It's purely an agreement to sell.
Just like an option, I guess, to buy.
Yeah, exactly.
That's exactly what it is, an option to buy.
So you're basically pitching the combined businesses before even rolling them up.
Well, so that's the key point.
So what you're going to do is find different types of buyers and some of them will be really annoyed that you've just put two businesses together and pitched them together.
Other people will see the value in having it not already been integrated because they can make the cost savings themselves.
So if both of these businesses are 1 million EBITDA, they can go out and make both these businesses 1 1/2 million EBITDA just by doing the back end stuff.
You're saying combine, combine the businesses right up front into a, basically facilitate a merger between the two of them and then be able to shop them so they're combined.
So it's not like putting it together on paper.
It's actually merging them together, facilitating savings and efficiencies and all that stuff.
That, that's the next step.
So you don't have to do all of the integration.
What I would suggest is there's a, there's probably a better middle ground than doing that.
So we speak to investment bankers that just this one guy who's got nine agencies that have nothing to do with each other, but he's shopping them around to sell them.
But what I would suggest is that you would do some initial work, like a very light touch, but pre integration work.
So basically you want to know what everybody's back office is running on.
You want to see where the cost savings can be made and you want to get that entire story right.
There's not necessarily that much financial investment.
It's more time.
But you can put that story on somebody's desk, you know, when, when it comes time to pitch and they want to do the acquisition and sell that as part of the thing.
Look, here's the map.
We've got the map already.
We know exactly what the integration is going to look like.
You just need to do it and make the savings yourself.
And that would be attractive to a lot of private equity in particular who are looking for a platform in the events space.
Yeah, and so the fee gets, so the compensation kicks in when the secondary transaction takes place.
You just distract.
You're skipping a spot, aren't you?
You're not doing the first Transaction you're skipping to the second.
Yeah.
Right, Right.
But your payday comes off the uplift.

So if these guys had have sold here where you've made them nothing on the the 5x if you get a deal done at 8x then that extra 3x multiple arbitrage that you facilitated, you take a percentage just off that.
So these guys aren't even losing anything.
Yeah.
Get agreement with you because if you never sell it then the, the trigger never gets pulled.
Interesting.
Have you done that before that kind of transaction where you cobble companies?
We haven't done the transaction so this is the first time we've done them for.
But we've worked on other transactions where other rollup people are putting together a virtual roll up.
So.
Yeah, I've seen it happen a few times.
Yeah it's fairly common in the, in the investment banker world.
Interesting.
It's kind of like a private sponsor but you, you're basically loading the gun but you're not pulling the trigger.
You're just the loaded gun to somebody else.
Yeah.
And which, so would you.
You would invest the time in.
In facilitating to you know getting those transactions papered and ready.
You know the trigger transaction.
So what kind of time frame do you think something like that would take before you get to a payday down the line?
Probably a couple years.
Right.
Not for us but this is what we do all the time.
So we're shopping deals around the marketing deals.
So on a, on a good day it would take about six months to get a deal done.
Postman getting bit by the dog about six.
Six months start to finish is kind of our, our track record.
It's actually pretty good to.
To you got.
I guess the key is to get these of the two companies have to be of like minds that they, they want to see that that exit.
Right.
Because at the end of the day that's.
So I'll give you another example and maybe there's an opportunity for us to work together on these things.
So I was approached by somebody who owns an event staffing company.
You know, field marketing staff, things like that.
Been in business a while.
I've known him on and off for about 20 years and looking to sell but realizes that there's probably a much greater exit opportunity to facilitate some kind of a roll up.
And he's spoken to two or three what I guess I would call friendly competitors who are of similar mindset and places in their careers.
They seem pretty interested.
They're you know that business is much more uniform.
You know the staffing Model is pretty turnkey wherever you go.
I mean, some places still do treat them as contractors, but these guys treat them as employees.
I mean, there's a couple of nuances here and there, but then the day you're renting labor, you know, by hour or day rates, and so he's interested in doing that.
And, you know, my initial thought was that I would have to find a.
Get him to hire me, you know, pay a fee to kind of find a buyer for him and then that the private equity firm was going to probably then take it over from there and then run the roll up.
But I could, I could much more easily deliver what you describe on, on a number of.
Like, I've got a lot of these.
They're like puzzle pieces.
These, these agencies I'm speaking to and as I speak to them, like, oh, you know who.
Those guys would buy them and those guys would buy them and, and these two should come together because this guy's a great salesperson, but he doesn't know how to run a team.
And these guys run a great team, but they need a good punter, you know, salesperson.

And I can see all these opportunities to facilitate and, and I think there are a number of situations where the owners are kind of, they've hit a wall, so to speak, and they are trying to figure out what's next or, you know, how to get a bigger payday or what have you.
And you know, I just don't think that the, the, you know, the, the traditional payment structure that Oakland operates on is, Is going to fly with a lot of these companies based on the size.
But there's, I know there's increased appetite certainly from private equity firms in the event space.
A lot of them that have never invested in this space are putting money in there.
You know, the current geopolitical economic shit show coming out of Washington notwithstanding, you know, the, the, the fundamentals of face to face events are pretty rock solid.
And you know, brands and organizations are still pretty, pretty strongly behind them and the space is still pretty fragmented.
So, you know, would you be.
I know you, your focus is not just the venue.
It's much broader.
It's, you know, probably more marketing agencies of all different stripes.
We're right across the board.
I mean, funnily enough, I did start out in events agencies with my M.
A stuff.
My, my very first client was an events company.
And so everybody that we targeted was pretty much in the event space.
So.
Yeah, but we've broadened, we've broadened it much further right now.
But Definitely, definitely.
I've got an interest in the event space and I agree with you as well.
I mean we've just done an immersive.
Well, we started an immersive roll up.
We're on agency number four.
Hopefully if we can close in the next couple of weeks with immersive stuff.
And this is exactly the script that we're running is that events is where it's at.
And obviously immersive and mixed reality events are the future.
And so we have a client that's, that's doing one of these at the moment.
That stuff, I love that stuff.
Not even necessarily from events.
Like there's just the ability to make museums more immersive and interactive and have, you know, be able to tell stories that are really, really engaging and immersive.
Is the technology is just getting better so fast.
There's a lot of opportunity there.
Yeah, yeah, you'll probably enjoy working on that one actually.
Yeah, you know, there's, you're probably familiar with the World Experience Organization.
You know, they've got, I think they have like Experiential week is coming up in London in, you know, later, later this spring.
But, you know, so how do we work together on something like this?
I mean, I think we.

It seems like you're of the same, you know, position that I'm in in terms of seeing the opportunity to build and add value by strategically bringing the right groups of people together and you know, forming, you know, one plus one equals three situations.
Do you, do you have any foothold in the United States or do you.
Most of our work is, is in the United States, so.
But I would definitely be interested in doing something.
We just need to figure out how it can work.
So it kind of depends on who's running what and who's doing the bits.
So for instance, let me tell you about my team on Agency A, which is the roll up that we're doing.
So I have somebody who usually works with us as a senior advisor.
She's extremely experienced in the immersive space.
Actually she's done.
She was MD at the, at the mill in New York and so she's got a big network and is well respected as well.
She does all of the, we do all of the, the outbound.
So we go out and find the target.
So I've got a team that works on that all the time.
So we're bringing in interested people.
She does those initial calls with them, kind of screens them, makes sure that they are good options for us.
But also pitch is the big idea.
And Then I get on a call with them and we go through kind of the nitty gritty, make sure that we've got a match and that everybody's aligned before we move on to the next bit.
But once we've got somebody signed up into the roll up, we then have somebody who's a former COO of a big agency in Los Angeles and he comes in and does the light integration aspects of it.
And so we're moving them through a funnel during a sort of three to six month period where they are aligning with the other people that are members in, in their group.
And so that is managed by the rest of my team.
So by the time we get to the point where we're ready, you know, we've got enough businesses in the roll up and we're ready to go out to market.
The, the businesses already kind of know each other.
We've done a bit of work and we've started to put together all the pitch pack and the IM or SIM to go to market with, which again is done, done by my team.
So I've got a lot of the sort of support in, in place to do the boring stuff.
But it sounds like where your, your power is is that you've got the network to pull these people in and, and start building the group.
So I just wonder whether it's maybe, maybe more of the back end stuff that we could potentially do with you because you've got the front end under control.

I mean at least the, the first half of it and then the piece where we go back out to market with the integrated or sort of pre integrated business, we could then, we could then do that piece of it as well on pitch the business and get the business.
Yeah, I think that that sounds right.
I mean where I could use the most help is in structuring these deals.
And you know, if you've got a, a good COO that becomes like a, an operator that streamlines some of these, these deals.
I mean, I guess that happens once the companies actually do combine as opposed to just having an option to, to purchase them.

You know, if you've got that process in place, that would be super helpful, you know, to be able to run, identify the, you know, two, three companies that would be good fit together and then just run them through that, that roadmap, that blueprint that you've got.
You know, what kind of upfront investment do you need to make or what I need to make?
You know, the, the CO that you mentioned about running, you know, efficiencies and Getting them integrated and the legal and accounting work.
I mean are there upfront costs that you typically incur on these things?
Where do you have the companies foot the bill for those as part of the process?
Yeah, so, so each company that comes into the roll ups, they pay a fee to come on board and that covers majority of our costs.
You know, the aim is to get somewhere around five of those businesses in and then that gives you a small amount of money to, to get some of the, the back end integrations done.
What do you typically ask them to, to commit to in terms of the payment?
So it's £25,000 and around 30 something USD.
So the rate that's really not that much.
I mean for, for their, what they're getting out of that.
I mean I'm just putting my hat on.
If I was a, if I had my first agency I, I, I would have paid that to have someone like you facilitate a, you know, some type of a merger or roll up or.
Yeah, so, so everybody that comes into that and you know, bear in mind we, we're shooting for 1 million EBITDA businesses as well.
Everybody that comes into that is set to make at least 2 to 4 million dollars off the back of, of of that.
So it's well, it's well worth the, the investment.
Even if it didn't happen, there would be a ton of upside to it.
Yeah, so it's a, it's a great investment.
And then we take, obviously we take as capital a, we take 5% on the transaction when we get the deal closed.
Although that's on a layman's scale as well.
So it gets smaller towards the top end.
That, that seems low though.
I mean for, for the work that you're doing, the 5%.
When we take 5% on a transaction, I mean we, we do that as an M and A company every day.
So that's all right.
But I don't know if you know somebody that's charging more than that, but.
No, no, but, but you're, from what I'm hearing you're doing more than just a straight transaction.

You know, you're, you're, you're facilitating integration and you know, I just envision that that's quite a bit more work than a traditional single seller client retaining you for an M and A transaction.
The economics of it is about the same for us.
So we roughly charge $30,000 and 5% on the deal just to do an M and A process.
So it's usually a six month process and 5% on the transaction.
So it's pretty close to that.
The only difference is in this instance, because we're running the whole process, we're finding everybody that goes into it.
We also take 20% on the upside as well.
So that arbitrage that we.
Okay, that makes sense, right?
Yeah, that's our payday.
Obviously, I've got different teams doing different of it.
So my team that will eventually take it to market and sell it, they're the same team that take all of our deals to market and sell it.
Whereas the actual integration piece of it and the, you know, the, the, the upside is created by a more senior group of people.
So.
Yeah, okay, that, that makes sense that the 20%, I didn't, I didn't factor in.
Yeah.
So that I would love to, to figure out what the next steps are for something like this.
I mean, I'm going to, I'm going to start putting some thoughts together on some of the pieces that I think would be easier to put together.

But I, there are a number of people who are kind of eager to go and would, you know, like I said, I've got two in particular that are really almost identical in size, a little bit different in, in functionality.
One's more creative, one's more technical.
But, you know, if they're each doing a million five in Ebitda, just for example, they're worth X.
If they're, you know, maybe they're doing five, maybe they get sold for five times.
Since your point, we combine them and you get 3 million and then you figure maybe you get another million in savings, I don't know, maybe less.
Now you're selling a business that's, you know, three and a half to 4 million in EBITDA.
And to your point, set of 5X, maybe now you're getting 8X or whatever.
Yeah, exactly.
Well, it is exactly how it works down the lower end.
It is, it's, it's there for founders to, to make a killing with people like us being able to piece these things together and take them to market.
So, yeah, it's much better for them to take the second bite of the cherry the first time.
Yeah, got it.
All right, so in those cases there, it sounds like the first step is they're not, they're not actually selling the business.
They're combining with the intention of having the combined business go to market as a, as a larger entity.
Yeah, but again, it's only a philosophical combining.
There is no actual structure that changes any of that.
I mean, there are different flavors of this and it really does depend on the people that, that come in.
But certainly there's a holding company which you, you have to maintain at least 20% of that.
You don't want to get diluted beyond, but you want to keep control of all votes in the holding company.

If you want to put eight other businesses in, you know, with a, a piece of the holding company as well and sell that combined, if that's what makes everybody more comfortable, then that is also an approach to take as well.
But yes, essentially you're, you're, you're in control of the, the holding company and that's what has the trigger options to buy out completely all the other businesses that are in the group.
Do you have a time frame for that trigger to kick in?
So yeah, so our time frames usually operate around the six month mark, so sometimes they can drag on.
So what I would say is it will possibly take us about six months to close an eight agency and that's kind of the max that I would want to put in.
Around 8 at 1 million EBITDA each changes the economics completely.
So that's as, as, as, as many as you'd need.
So it'd take probably about six months to find all of those.
Then once you have them and the group's formed, then it's another six months to go to market, find a buyer, close the deal, do all of the due diligence, etc.
Yeah.
So possibly from today would be 12 months to start from a standing start.
Right.
But you have more than like, if it takes an extra year, I assume you have the, your option to sell that combined entity doesn't expire.
No.
You'd want to get like three years on it.
Yeah.
Okay, that's what I thought.
Got it.
Okay, so then when you mentioned the COO that goes over integration and efficiencies and all that, that's just blueprinting it, not necessarily actually facilitating it.
Right.
There's not an announced merger.
There's not, you know, PR behind it.
You don't have actual, you know, staffing changes or org chart changes or any of that.
Yet you're kind of mapping out what it would look like when it's combined.
Yeah, exactly.
So I mean it again, it's varied on the different roll ups I've worked on depending on the personalities involved.
Sometimes there's a clear standout CEO that should be CEO of the group.
You can start warming them up.
You'll find that other founders want to leave or they want to take a step back earlier.
So certainly those conversations can be started and Also again, it depends on the personalities.
If they are happy to start the pre integration stuff, then you should get some of it started.

I mean if, you know, if some people are on Salesforce and somebody else is on another CRM and it just makes sense to, to bring everybody over or whatever it is, the small changes where you're just aligning everybody's tech stacks and aligning the accounting software and you know, you're starting to bring some of those things together.
But again, it depends on time frame and personalities and whether you would want to get into all of that stuff.
But that's why we want to bring with us our COO to do all of that stuff.
Who can manage it over a six month period where we're nudging people down a funnel, down a road together.
So by the time we get the transaction closed that you're already on the path.
And it's a much sexier proposition for a buyer to know that everybody's kind of aligned.
We've got it all mapped out, we've started some of the basic stuff, that sort of thing.
So people, the, the owners are basically committing to merging.
Yeah.
Regardless of when a buyer gets facilitated or is that okay?
Yeah, yeah.
I mean you're going to get a buyer, it's just time.
Have you had any situations where the combined business is not fetching the, the multiple that the, that the owners were expecting just economic downturns or I don't know, market conditions changing?
I haven't personally, not yet, but I haven't done one myself.
The companies that we've worked in, we've seen all sorts of problems.
There's all sorts of stuff that can go wrong.
I mean it's just being able to mitigate against anything going wrong.

The biggest problem is volume of deal flow because what's happening more or less all of the roll ups that I've seen that have been virtual roll ups like this you've situation where at least one founder has walked before the deal got done.
And what, what's the main reason that they, that they walk.
They just personality clashes, co fee, egos, you know, changing in revenues, going in the wrong direction, losing confidence.
Loads of different reasons.
Thanks.
So they, they guess the, the terms of the initial transaction is gives an owner the ability to just kind of pull out for whatever reason.
So they're pretty tight normally.
But the thing is, I mean particularly in Europe where I've seen it happen more often where somebody's walked you, it's harder to, to get the legal.
What.
Would you call it Force.
There is no legal force majeure, whatever.
Yeah.
To force somebody to sell if they refuse.
So it just isn't there.
There's no way to do it.
But pretty much I would say most people are happy to.
I mean, that's why they've got into it, They've invested in it.
Right.
And all the other stuff that comes with it.
So, yeah, I think it's a great opportunity.
It sounds like these two companies that you have is exactly what I'm talking about in terms of the opportunity there.
I mean, that is something you can just take straight to market pretty much without too much.
